design_detail: Retrospective review of coroners' cases from the Victorian State Coroner, Australia (J Anal Toxicol 2011;35:219-226; printed pp. 219-226, read as the published PDF). Closed cases from January 2002 to December 2008 were found through the National Coroners Information System where postmortem blood held a quantified MDMA result above 0.02 mg/L: 106 cases among 14,682 coroners' cases with full toxicology (p. 223). Pathology, toxicology, coroners' findings and case circumstances were read for each. The authors examined in detail only the 19 cases in which they judged the drug combination able to cause serotonin toxicity or another adverse drug reaction, and sorted them by the risk level given in a drug-interaction database (Table I, p. 220): 4 major (all with moclobemide), 10 moderate (dothiepin, methamphetamine and other amphetamines, tramadol, venlafaxine, methadone, fluoxetine) and 5 minor (citalopram, sertraline, fluvoxamine, doxylamine). The other 87 (MDMA alone or with its metabolite MDA 20; MDMA with ethanol 34; MDMA with other drugs judged unlikely to interact 33) were not analysed further (p. 223). Table II (pp. 221-223) lists, for each of the 19, sex, age, cause of death and autopsy findings, the drugs found with their blood concentrations, and the specimen and estimated postmortem interval. No comparison group and no count of people who took the same drugs and survived.
can_establish: Which medicines and other drugs were found, alongside MDMA, in 19 deaths in Victoria in 2002-2008 that the authors selected for a possible drug interaction, the cause of death and autopsy findings recorded for those 19, and how the 106 deaths with a quantified MDMA result divided into MDMA alone, MDMA with alcohol, MDMA with other drugs judged unlikely to interact, and the 19 selected.
cannot_establish: How often any medicine is present in deaths involving MDMA (the 19 were picked for having such a drug), that any medicine caused or contributed to any death, how risky any combination is (there is no count of the people who took the same combination and did not die), or where the medicines came from (usually not known). It does not show that MDMA caused the death in the 106 cases, 60% of which were deaths from external injury.

sample.recruitment: Not recruited: closed Victorian coroners' cases, January 2002 to December 2008, found through the National Coroners Information System, with a quantified MDMA result above 0.02 mg/L in postmortem blood (Cohort selection, p. 220). In Victoria all violent, unexpected and suspicious deaths reported to the coroner receive a full medicolegal investigation (Toxicological analysis, p. 220).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: the 106 cases above, among 14,682 coroners' cases with full toxicology. Examined in detail: cases 'demonstrating a risk' of serotonin toxicity or another adverse drug reaction from the drug combination and the circumstances; the others were left out 'because this cohort focused on toxic drug combinations only' (p. 223).
sample.demographics: All 106: 83 (78%) male; ages 17 to 48, median 25; 64 (60%) died by external injury, for example hangings and motor vehicle crashes (p. 223). The 19: 14 male; ages 21 to 45, median 28 (p. 224).
sample.selection_effects: The 19 were chosen by the authors' own judgment of interaction risk from the drugs found and the circumstances, so every one of them has a drug of interest by design; 87 of the 106 were set aside and the contents of the 33 'other drugs' cases are not listed. Only deaths with MDMA quantified above 0.02 mg/L in blood are in the 106, so deaths in which MDMA was not tested for or not found are absent. Because 60% of the 106 died of external injury, they are not all deaths from drug toxicity. Counts of medicines among the 19 describe those 19; they are not a rate for deaths involving MDMA.

exposure.measurement: Postmortem toxicology: an immunoassay screen of blood (ELISA) or urine (CEDIA) for amphetamines, benzodiazepines, cannabis metabolites, cocaine metabolites and opiates, plus a semiquantitative gas chromatography screen for common drugs; positive findings confirmed by quantitative gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (lower limit of quantitation for MDMA 0.02 mg/L). Femoral-vein blood was used unless stated, to limit redistribution (Methods, p. 220). Concentrations are in mg/L, except ethanol (g/100 mL), THC (ng/mL) and carbon monoxide (% saturation) (Table II footnote).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not known: only concentrations measured after death are given, not how much was taken, when or how. MDMA concentrations in the 19 ranged from 0.02 to 3.5 mg/L (Group 1: 1.0 to 2.6, median 1.85; Group 2: 0.02 to 3.5, median 0.07; Group 3: 0.2 to 1.4, median 0.2; p. 224). These are measurements after death, not doses.
exposure.polysubstance: The study is about combinations: every one of the 19 had at least one other drug (a median of 4 substances other than MDMA, editors' count from Table II). Methamphetamine or amphetamine was found in 15 of the 19, in all three risk groups; THC in 5 and ethanol in 3. The paper does not weigh how much each substance contributed to a death.

comparison.controls: None. The only comparison is with the 87 cases set aside, whose contents are counted (20, 34 and 33) but not listed, so the 19 cannot be compared with deaths involving MDMA without these drugs or with people who took the same drugs and survived.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Medical history, prescriptions, the source of the drugs, the timing of medicines relative to MDMA and whether medicines were taken as prescribed are mostly missing (Limitations, p. 225); most deaths were unwitnessed, so symptoms before death are rarely known.

outcomes.instruments: Cause of death and intent as recorded by pathologists and coroners; autopsy in 16 of the 19 with the findings in Table II; clinical signs of serotonin toxicity noted by a paramedic or physician in 3 cases (p. 224); the authors' ratings of interaction risk from Micromedex Drugdex and other references (p. 223).
outcomes.validity_norms: Serotonin toxicity cannot be shown at autopsy; the diagnosis rests on witnessed symptoms, the drugs involved and the circumstances (p. 220). Postmortem redistribution can raise concentrations: cavity blood in cases 1 and 10 and a six-day interval before sampling in case 18; tolerance makes concentrations of morphine hard to interpret (p. 225). Codeine and morphine in Table II are unconjugated drug only.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Interaction risk' means the authors' Group 1 (major), 2 (moderate) or 3 (minor) in Table I. Cause of death is the coroner's wording in Table II.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; the authors assessed each case individually with the findings in hand (Data analysis, p. 220).

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive counts only, no tests or intervals. Of 106 cases: 4 major-risk (moclobemide), 10 moderate and 5 minor; 87 set aside (20 MDMA alone or with MDA, 34 with ethanol, 33 with other drugs judged unlikely to interact), that is about 19, 32 and 31 in 100 of the 106 for the three set-aside groups and 18 in 100 for the 19 examined (editors' arithmetic). Editors' tallies of Table II (19 cases; cases with at least one substance of the class): methamphetamine or amphetamine 15 (methamphetamine 14, amphetamine 7); any antidepressant 13 (moclobemide 4; fluoxetine, sertraline, dothiepin, venlafaxine, citalopram, mirtazapine or fluvoxamine 9); any opioid including the heroin marker 6-MAM 12 (methadone 5, codeine 5, morphine 5, tramadol 1, 6-MAM 3); any benzodiazepine or metabolite 8; benzodiazepine or opioid 14; paracetamol or ibuprofen 4; THC 5; ethanol 3. Cause of death: drug toxicity alone 12 (cases 1-5, 7, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18, 19); injury with combined toxicity 2 (cases 13, 17); other causes 5 (drowning, train impact, haemorrhagic shock with incised wounds, hanging, carbon monoxide). Serotonin toxicity was noted by a paramedic or physician before death in 3 of the 4 moclobemide cases (cases 1 to 3). MDMA at or below 0.05 mg/L in 5 of the 10 Group 2 cases (6, 8, 9, 13, 14).
analysis.preregistration_detail: None; descriptive retrospective review with ethics approval from the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine and the Department of Justice (p. 223).
analysis.selective_reporting: The 19 cases are chosen by the authors' judgment, and the risk grouping follows the pharmaceutical drug (Table I rates amphetamine derivatives as moderate, yet they appear in 4 of the major and 3 of the minor cases). The examples of major and minor risk in the text (chlorpromazine and chlorpheniramine) do not appear in Table I or II.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 19 deaths the authors selected from 106 for a possible drug interaction, every one had at least one other drug: methamphetamine or amphetamine in 15, antidepressants in 13 (moclobemide in 4, with signs of serotonin toxicity noted before death in 3 of those 4), opioids in 12 (3 with the heroin marker 6-MAM), benzodiazepines in 8. Twelve of the 19 died of drug toxicity alone; the others died of injury or other causes with drugs present. In the other 87 of the 106 (82 in 100), MDMA was found alone or with MDA (20), with ethanol (34) or with drugs judged unlikely to interact (33).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors conclude that some people may combine pharmaceutical drugs with MDMA to enhance the effect or ease the comedown, that this appeared a limited practice in Victoria in 2002-2008, that serotonin toxicity was probably overlooked, that knowledge of interactions is probably limited and that education is needed (pp. 224-225). The case counts and postmortem concentrations do not show intentions, knowledge or whether serotonin toxicity occurred in the cases where it was not recorded; the paper gives a source for the drugs only for two moclobemide cases (witness statements suggesting a friend or family member). The abstract's '43 (41%)' cases of combined use cannot be matched to the results (19 + 33 = 52).

timeline.event: Case report of a death after MDMA and moclobemide (Vuori et al.); one of the cases the authors cite for the combination.
Qualitative review of serotonin syndrome with MDMA and other serotonergic drugs (Silins et al.); the authors take part of their risk grouping from it.
This case series: 19 of 106 Victorian deaths with MDMA in blood, 2002-2008, examined for drug combinations.

replication.where_it_stands: A descriptive series from one Australian state; it is not designed to be replicated and the authors say a national search would find more. The four moclobemide cases are examined in a separate publication the authors cite (p. 224), which was not read.

funding.funder: Not reported: there is no funding statement. The acknowledgments thank the National Coroners Information System, the State Coroner's Office, the pathologists, technicians and toxicologists of the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine, and a colleague for help with the manuscript (p. 225).
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated; the paper has no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: The authors are in the Department of Forensic Medicine at Monash University and at the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine, whose staff are thanked for help with the cases (p. 219, p. 225).

what_would_settle_it: A study across all Australian states or several years that counts every death and compares it with a denominator (people presenting to hospital after MDMA, or a cohort of people taking MDMA), with the content of what was taken confirmed, prescribing and dispensing records, the timing of each medicine, clinical data such as temperature, a fixed postmortem sampling site and interval, and a rule for rating interaction risk set in advance and applied without knowledge of the outcome.

domains.note: The 19 were chosen by the authors' judgment of interaction risk from 106; 87 were set aside and the 33 'other drugs' cases are not listed; only deaths with MDMA above 0.02 mg/L in blood are in the 106.

Immunoassay screen and quantitative GC-MS, but postmortem redistribution (cavity blood in cases 1 and 10; six-day interval in case 18), unconjugated-only opiates and tolerance limit what the concentrations mean; MDMA is printed as 0.02 mg/L for case 13, equal to the cut-off.

domains.domain: Judgment of interaction risk and cause of death
domains.note: Risk groups were assigned by the authors from a drug database with the findings in hand; serotonin toxicity cannot be shown postmortem and was recorded before death in only 3 cases.
The source of the drugs, prescriptions, timing, clinical data and medical history are mostly missing (p. 225); most deaths were unwitnessed.
The abstract's 43 (41%) cases cannot be matched to the results; pulmonary oedema is in 4 cases in the text and 5 in Table II; named examples (chlorpromazine, chlorpheniramine) are not in the tables.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a coroners' case series (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The series is a transparent list of what was found in 19 deaths chosen for possible interactions, and the table can be cited as a description of those 19. It cannot be cited for how often medicines are found in deaths involving MDMA, for the risk of any combination, or for any medicine having caused a death. A claim resting only on this series stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: Abstract: 106 fatalities with a quantified MDMA result were identified in Victorian coroners' closed cases, 2002-2008; the abstract states that 43 (41%) involved MDMA with other drugs, including pharmaceuticals likely to result in an adverse drug reaction or varying risks (4 high-risk cases with moclobemide, 10 moderate-risk and 5 minor-risk); it concludes that potential interactions between MDMA and pharmaceutical preparations, in particular serotonin toxicity, should be recognised and publicised.
key_findings.note: 43 (41%) cannot be matched to the Results (19 + 33 = 52).

key_findings.finding: Methods: postmortem femoral blood was used where possible; immunoassay screening (ELISA blood or CEDIA urine) for amphetamines, benzodiazepines, cannabis metabolites, cocaine metabolites and opiates, a semiquantitative gas chromatography screen, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry confirmation (MDMA lower limit of quantitation 0.02 mg/L). Cases came from the National Coroners Information System: closed Victorian cases, January 2002 to December 2008, with MDMA above 0.02 mg/L in postmortem blood. Each case was assessed for toxicology, pathology and circumstances, including the risk of serotonin toxicity from monoamine oxidase inhibitors, SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol, ethanol, amphetamines and some antihistamines.
key_findings.locator: Methods: Toxicological analysis; Cohort selection; Data analysis

key_findings.finding: Table I, risk groups from Drugdex and other references: major (Group 1), moclobemide, a reversible MAO-A inhibitor (hypertensive crisis and serotonin toxicity); moderate (Group 2), dothiepin (tricyclic), amphetamine and derivatives (amphetamine, methamphetamine, MDA, MDEA), tramadol, venlafaxine and cocaine, and the CYP2D6 inhibitors methadone and fluoxetine; minor (Group 3), doxylamine and the SSRIs citalopram, sertraline and fluvoxamine.

Table II, the 19 cases with sex, age, cause of death and drugs in postmortem blood: cases 1 to 4 (Group 1) all had moclobemide with MDMA 1.0 to 2.6 mg/L; cases 5 to 14 (Group 2) and 15 to 19 (Group 3) are listed with their drugs. Editors' tallies: methamphetamine or amphetamine 15; antidepressants 13; opioids (including 6-MAM) 12; benzodiazepines or metabolites 8; paracetamol or ibuprofen 4; THC 5; ethanol 3. Sixteen of the 19 had a leg-blood specimen, 2 cavity blood and 1 antemortem serum; the estimated postmortem interval was 2 to 6 days.
key_findings.locator: Table II (cases 1-8 on p. 221; 9-16 on p. 222; 17-19 on p. 223)
key_findings.note: Tallies by the editors from the printed table; the paper does not tabulate them.

key_findings.finding: Selection and counts: the paper examined only cases demonstrating a risk of serotonin toxicity or another adverse drug reaction from the combination; the others were excluded because 'this cohort focused on toxic drug combinations only'. 106 cases among 14,682 coroners' cases with full toxicology; 83 (78%) male; 64 (60%) died by external injury; ages 17 to 48, median 25. 4 major, 10 moderate and 5 minor risk cases were examined; the other 87 were MDMA alone or with MDA as metabolite (20), MDMA with ethanol (34) or MDMA with other drugs not likely to cause an adverse drug reaction (33).
key_findings.locator: Methods: Data analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Results: Basic characteristics, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Toxicology in the 19: 14 male, ages 21 to 45 (median 28). Group 1: all four with moclobemide, MDMA 1.0 to 2.6 mg/L (median 1.85), clinical symptoms of serotonin toxicity noted by a paramedic or physician in three (cases 1 to 3). Group 2 (10 cases): fluoxetine, venlafaxine, methadone, dothiepin and tramadol, with methamphetamine and paramethoxyamphetamine; MDMA 0.02 to 3.5 mg/L (median 0.07). Group 3 (5 cases): citalopram, fluvoxamine, sertraline and/or doxylamine; MDMA 0.2 to 1.4 mg/L (median 0.2).
key_findings.locator: Results: Toxicology findings in the 19 cases of interest, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 223) to 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Pathology: 16 of the 19 had a full autopsy; coronary artery disease with significant occlusion in two (cases 2 and 4); ischaemic change in the myocardium in one (case 7); hepatic pathology (hepatitis C or fatty liver) in six (cases 1, 7, 8, 13, 18, 19); pulmonary oedema reported in four cases in the text (five in Table II: cases 1, 2, 4, 5, 7); the autopsy findings were relatively unremarkable in Groups 2 and 3 with no significant natural disease.
key_findings.locator: Results: Pathology findings in the cases of interest

key_findings.finding: Discussion: four cases combined MDMA with moclobemide, described as a high-risk combination for serotonin toxicity; Group 2 cases mostly involved serotonergic antidepressants or opioids; serotonin toxicity was reported before death in only three cases and the authors think it was more likely overlooked in others; several Group 2 cases involved benzodiazepines, which the authors say are often used in the days after ecstasy; methadone and fluoxetine are CYP2D6 inhibitors, which the authors say can raise MDMA concentrations; a 2006 survey found that over a quarter of the sample had used ecstasy with a pharmaceutical drug, most often from friends.

Source and limits: in many cases the source of the drugs is unknown; witness statements in a number of cases, including two of the moclobemide cases with fatal serotonin toxicity, suggested the person may have obtained the medicine from a friend or family member. Limitations named: postmortem redistribution (cavity blood in case 10; a six-day interval in case 18), missing information on the source of drugs, prescribing and clinical data, concentrations of drugs with tolerance such as morphine being hard to interpret, and a likely under-recording of non-fatal and serotonin toxicity cases.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph (begins on p. 224), 7th and 8th paragraphs (p. 225)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: some people may combine pharmaceutical drugs with MDMA to enhance the high or counteract a comedown, but this appeared to be a limited practice in Victoria in 2002-2008; there is a risk for people using pharmaceuticals therapeutically who take MDMA occasionally, particularly if unaware of interactions; since many deaths were apparently unintentional drug toxicity, the authors consider it likely that knowledge of interactions is limited.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 43 (41%) of the 106 cases involved MDMA with other drugs. The Results give 19 examined cases plus 33 cases with other drugs judged unlikely to interact (52), or 86 if the 34 with ethanol are added.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's headline share cannot be traced; use the Results counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The text names chlorpromazine as an example of a major interaction and chlorpheniramine as a minor one; neither appears in Table I or Table II.
reporting_issues.consequence: The examples describe the rating scheme, not the cases examined.

reporting_issues.issue: The text reports pulmonary oedema in four cases; Table II lists it in five (cases 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7).
reporting_issues.consequence: Counts from the text and the table disagree by one.

reporting_issues.issue: Table I places amphetamine and its derivatives in the moderate group, but methamphetamine or amphetamine appears in 4 major-group cases (1-4) and in 3 minor-group cases (15, 17, 19). The group follows the pharmaceutical drug.
reporting_issues.consequence: Group labels do not describe how many drugs of each risk were present.

reporting_issues.issue: The footnote to Table I says it includes all the drugs detected with MDMA in this cohort, but cocaine, MDEA and MDA appear in none of the 19 cases in Table II, and Table II lists drugs not in Table I (mirtazapine, olanzapine, ketamine, paramethoxyamphetamine, codeine, morphine, 6-MAM and all the benzodiazepines).
reporting_issues.consequence: Table I is a rating scheme, not a list of what was found.

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion rule is MDMA above 0.02 mg/L in postmortem blood, but case 13 is printed with MDMA 0.02 mg/L, and 5 of the 10 Group 2 cases have MDMA at or below 0.05 mg/L (cases 6, 8, 9, 13, 14).
reporting_issues.consequence: Several cases sit at the detection limit; MDMA may have been a minor finding in them.

reporting_issues.issue: The contents of the 33 cases of MDMA with 'other drugs not likely to cause an adverse drug reaction' are not given, although the 19 examined cases are chosen against them.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reader cannot see what the authors judged unlikely to interact.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 219-226 (PDFs/MDMA/Pilgrim_2011_MDMADeathsPharmaceuticals.pdf), full text including the reference list; extracted once with pdftotext; Table I (p. 220) and Table II (pp. 221-223) were transcribed and checked case by case against 110 dpi renderings of the pages.
